summary: Describes the URI resource record, a DNS record type that maps a hostname to one or more URIs. The record type had already been registered, and this document formally describes it, including how multiple entries are prioritized.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7553 describes a new kind of DNS record for storing the address of a service as a complete URI. The service and the protocol are written into the name being looked up, so a client that knows what it wants gets back exactly that one address, instead of a list of every address attached to the name. The document sets out the format of the record, how it relates to the older NAPTR and SRV records, and how it must be signed to avoid a downgrade attack.

questions: what is a uri dns record
subtitle: A DNS record type that answers "where is this service, for this protocol", with the address written out in full.

tldr.problem: The DNS already maps a domain name to the addresses of a service, but through NAPTR records that return every URI connected with a name, so a client has to pick the right one itself and then apply rewrite rules to get it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7553 defines a new record type, number 256, in which the service and protocol are encoded in the owner name and the full URI is the target, so a client that already knows which service it wants can ask for exactly that and get the address back as it stands.
tldr.outcome: The new record complements the older ones rather than replacing them: NAPTR is still how a client discovers which services exist, and the URI record is the second step, replacing SRV records in that step. The document also explains why the record has to be signed with DNSSEC to be safe.

facts.label: Fixed part of the data
facts.value: 4 octets: 2 for priority and 2 for weight

today: RFC 7553 is an Informational RFC published in June 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. The record type it describes was allocated by IANA before the document was published, and the document is the reference for that registration.

sections.title: What the Record Is For
sections.content:
The document explains how the Domain Name System can store URIs and how a hostname can be resolved to one for use by an application. For the resolution to work the application has to know two things: the hostname and the protocol the URI is to be used with, and the protocol is registered by IANA.

Historically, mapping a domain name to a URL has relied on the NAPTR record types and then on the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System framework, which uses the DNS as a database. That has consequences, one of which is that the set of records returned contains all the URIs connected with the owner, and not only the ones relating to a particular service.

The URI record lets the querying party do the equivalent of choosing which NAPTR record it is interested in and have only those returned. That works because the data in the service field of the NAPTR record is included in the owner part of the URI record. And because the URI record holds the target URI directly as part of its data, it is easy to extract the correct target, instead of applying rewrite rules as in NAPTR.

Querying for URI records does not replace querying for NAPTR records, nor the use of S-NAPTR. It is a complementary mechanism for when one already knows which service field is of interest, letting a client query directly for the specific subset of what would otherwise be a large set returned by a NAPTR query.
sections.plainLanguage: The older way of finding a service address in the DNS returns every address attached to a name, and the client has to work out which one it wants and how to rewrite it. The new record puts the service and protocol into the name being looked up, so the client asks for exactly the address it wants and gets it in final form.

sections.title: When It Applies
sections.content:
The expectation is that URI records will be used by clients for applications where the protocol to be used is already known but where an extra abstraction is needed to separate a domain name from a point of service, as the URI addresses. One example is an organisation that has many domain names but only one official web page.

Applications need to know the specific service to prepend to the hostname. Making repeated queries for URI records is not a replacement for querying for NAPTR records under the NAPTR or S-NAPTR algorithms. NAPTR records serve the purpose of discovering the various services, or the URIs, and of looking up access points for a given service. Those are two very different kinds of need, and the document keeps them apart: the URI record answers the second, while NAPTR answers the first.
sections.plainLanguage: The record suits a client that already knows which protocol and service it wants, but needs to keep the domain name and the point of service apart, such as a company with many domain names and one web page. It is the second step of a lookup, not the first: the first step is finding out which services exist at all.

sections.title: The Format of the Record
sections.content:
In presentation format the record has the owner name, a time to live, the class, the type, a priority, a weight and a target. The owner name follows special conventions. As with the SRV record, service information is encoded in the owner name using service parameters, which are those registered by IANA in the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry, or registered as Enumservices. The Enumservice parameters are reversed, so that subtypes come before the type, and are prepended with an underscore in separate labels before the owner name. The underscore avoids collisions with DNS labels that occur in nature, and reversing the order makes it possible to delegate to different zones, and therefore to different providers of DNS, if that is needed.

So a lookup for the URI of a service with the Enumservice parameter A:B:C for the host example.com queries the name _C._B._A.example.com with type URI, and a lookup for a service with the service name A and transport protocol B for the same host queries _A._B.example.com. The type number of the URI record is 256. The record is class independent and has no special time-to-live requirements.

The priority field holds the priority of the target URI in that record, in the range 0 to 65535. A client must attempt to contact the URI with the lowest-numbered priority it can reach, and URIs with the same priority should be selected according to the probabilities defined by the weight field. The weight field is the server selection mechanism, giving a relative weight for entries with the same priority, where larger weights should be given a proportionately higher probability of being selected; its range is also 0 to 65535.

The target field holds the URI enclosed in double-quote characters, in the form given in RFC 3986, and the URI is resolved according to the definitions for its scheme. Because the URI is not encoded as a character-string, there is no 255-character size limitation, and the target must not be an empty URI. On the wire, the data of the record consists of a 2-octet priority field, a 2-octet weight field and a variable-length target field. The priority and the weight are unsigned integers in network byte order, and the remaining data is the target as a sequence of octets without the enclosing quotes. The length of the target field must be greater than zero. The record causes no additional section processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is named after the service and protocol, so a lookup for the web service over TCP asks for _http._tcp.example.com. The data it carries is a priority, a weight and the URI itself, in the same order and with the same meaning as the fields of the older SRV record, except that the last one is a full address rather than a host name and a port.

sections.title: How It Sits With the Older Records
sections.content:
An organisation with the domain names example.com and example.net whose FTP archive is at ftp://ftp1.example.com/public can publish the record under the service name ftp and the transport protocol tcp, taken from the IANA registry, in both zones. Each zone then holds the same owner name with the same priority of 10, weight of 1 and the same target URI.

The URI record type is not a replacement for S-NAPTR. It is an extension, and the second step of the S-NAPTR resolution can resolve a URI record instead of using SRV records and yet another algorithm for how to use those records for the specific protocol. The example given puts a NAPTR record in place for the service, pointing at _http._tcp.example.com, and a URI record under that name holding the address.

The URI record type together with S-NAPTR can be viewed as a replacement for U-NAPTR. The URI record type is only of interest when one knows a base domain name, a protocol and a service, so that the record to look up can be composed. NAPTR records of any kind are used to look up what services exist for a certain domain, which is one step before the URI record is used. The URI record type can also be viewed as a replacement for the SRV record, because like it, it can only be looked up if one knows the base domain, the protocol and the service. It has similar functionality and uses the same registry for service names, but instead of returning a hostname and a port number it returns a full URI, so it can be seen as a more powerful resource record than SRV.
sections.plainLanguage: The new record is a second step, not a first one. The first step, asking what services exist, stays with the older NAPTR records. In the second step, the URI record replaces the SRV record, and returns the whole address instead of a host name and a port that the client would have to combine.

sections.title: Naming, Delegation and Registration
sections.content:
Using prefix labels, such as underscored service tags, for a specific owner name has a counter-intuitive effect when the owner name is a wildcard name. The example given is that _s2._s1.*.example.net is not a wildcard name and cannot be used to return a synthesised answer for a query name of _s2._s1.a.example.net. Besides that, underscored service tags used for the URI record, which are based on the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry, may have slightly different semantics from service tags used for other, as yet unspecified, record types, which can cause subtle management problems when a delegation structure developed for URI records is also used for other types. Because the service labels might be overloaded, applications should check carefully that the application-level protocol is indeed the protocol they expect. There may also be management issues when the delegations from a service to sub-service labels involve several parties and different stakeholders.

The record type itself was allocated by IANA after an expert review in February 2011, in the registry of resource record types, and the reference for that registration has been updated to point at this document. No new registry is needed for services, because the Service Name, Transport Protocol Port Numbers, Enumservices and DNS SRV Service Type registries are used for the URI record type as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Two practical notes. Service labels in the name behave oddly with wildcards, so a wildcard entry under an underscored service tag will not answer for a name beneath it. And because the same set of service names is shared with other record types, an application should check that the protocol it finds is the one it asked for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using the URI record together with a security mechanism that relies on verifying the authentication of hostnames, such as TLS, makes it important to choose the correct domain name when making the comparison and to ensure that the change of hostname is secured by DNSSEC, so that it can be trusted in the same way as a redirect in HTTP over TLS. If the URI record is not signed with DNSSEC and then validated successfully, trusting the unsigned URI effectively leads to a downgrade attack.

The basic mechanism for using the record successfully runs in four steps. The domain announces in DNS that it is hosted somewhere else, with some URI. The URI record is secured with DNSSEC, which is best done by validating in the application doing the lookup, but could also be done in the local recursive resolver or in a trusted recursive resolver that is also validating, according to the local trust policy. The client then verifies that the TLS certificate for the connection matches, using the hostname in the URI and not the hostname that was originally looked up. If needed, application-layer authentication is done over the encrypted connection.

The URI in the record may also contain errors. Applications using the record for resolution should behave as they would if the user had typed, or copied and pasted, the URI, and at least it must be clear to the user that the error is not on their side. A URI used in a record should not include user information, since data in the DNS must be viewed as publicly available information.
sections.plainLanguage: The record points the client at a different host name, and that host name has to be checked against the certificate the client then receives. If the record itself is not signed, an attacker could change it and the check would be worthless, which is why the document insists on signing the record and validating the signature.

data.title: example.com and example.net
data.code:
$ORIGIN example.com.
_ftp._tcp    IN URI 10 1 "ftp://ftp1.example.com/public"

$ORIGIN example.net.
_ftp._tcp    IN URI 10 1 "ftp://ftp1.example.com/public"

viz.caption: HOW THE URI RECORD FITS WITH THE OLDER RECORD TYPES

items.title: NAPTR
items.text: Used to look up what services exist for a domain, one step before the URI record is used. The set returned holds every URI connected with the owner.

items.title: S-NAPTR
items.text: The second step of the discovery process. The URI record extends it, so that step can resolve a URI record instead of an SRV record.

items.title: U-NAPTR
items.text: The URI record type together with S-NAPTR can be viewed as a replacement for it.

items.title: SRV
items.text: The URI record can be viewed as a replacement, using the same registry of service names but returning a full URI instead of a host name and a port.

items.title: The URI record
items.text: Only of interest when the base domain, the protocol and the service are already known, so that the name to look up can be composed.
